reason: The court did place the burden for fraud or undue influence on the objectors, but the statement drops the prior will-propounder burden and suspicion-removal context.
The court found no well-grounded suspicion on the evidence, but did not hold that such suspicion is a general prerequisite to challenging a will's authenticity.
The holding was confined to a Primary Court's duty under section 66 before a possession inquiry, while the statement states it too broadly as a duty of any court.
The quote supports a condition precedent, but only for the Primary Court's section 66(7) inquiry after failed settlement efforts, which the statement omits.
The statement is a vague description of one step in the statutory possession inquiry rather than the court's holding.
The court treated the undisputed survey report as decisive on these facts, not as a general rule that a Commissioner's report determines the corpus.
This merely repeats a factual comment about the plaintiff's failure to act under section 5 and is not a legal holding.
The judgment faulted ignoring a relevant survey report in this partition case, but the statement is an overbroad generalization.
The court expressly held that due execution of the deed was proved on a balance of probability and used that standard to dismiss the appeal.
The court held that non-observance of Notaries Ordinance section 31 rules did not invalidate the deed because section 33 protected it.
The court stated as its own view that due execution essentially required compliance with section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance.
The court used this rule to reject the argument that omission from testamentary inventory defeated the deceased owner's title and his heirs' rights.
This is only statutory background about interlocutory decrees and omits the decisive outside-corpus limitation.
The court construed section 18(a)(viii) as making the Commissioner include existing access from the nearest public road in the report.
The actual holding was that the District Court could not adjudicate a roadway outside the partition corpus, not a road outside its jurisdiction.
The court held that the notarial lease completed after registration of the partition lis pendens was void under sections 66(1) and 66(2).
The quoted point is an evidential finding that this tenant's monthly tenancy predated the lease, not a general legal rule.
The ratio was that this tenant could rely on a valid prior monthly tenancy not referable to the void lease, which the statement dilutes into a broad proposition.
The court held that compromise in a partition action is possible after title investigation and satisfaction as to the parties' rights.
Strict compliance with Civil Procedure Code sections 91 and 408 was part of the court's reason for setting aside the imprecise compromise decree.
The court treated prior investigation of title as the trial judge's obligation before permitting a partition compromise.
The court allowed ejectment without a prayer for declaration only where title was pleaded in the plaint and tried on accepted issues, which the statement omits.
The court expressly held that absence of a declaration-of-title prayer caused no prejudice where title was pleaded and accepted issues raised it.
This states the litigation contest rather than a rule, and section 3 of the Prescription Ordinance was not construed for that issue-framing statement.
The paper-title possession presumption was a holding, but the cited Prescription Ordinance section 3 relates to adverse possession rather than this presumption.
